index_record.dataset_generation_caption:
The figure illustrates the process of updating an empirical joint distribution in the ENMI2D algorithm by incorporating probability mass from corresponding pixel values in a captured image and a map section. The global layout consists of three main components arranged horizontally: on the left, two 3x3 grids labeled 'Captured Image Y' and 'Map Section Y^ℓ', stacked vertically; in the center, probability distributions derived from specific pixel positions in these grids; and on the right, a 4x4 grid representing the empirical joint distribution, labeled 'Distribution p̂(A, A^ℓ)', with axes labeled 'A' (horizontal, values 0–3) and 'A^ℓ' (vertical, values 0–3). 

In the left portion, the 'Captured Image Y' grid contains integer values ranging from 0 to 3, with the pixel at position (row 1, column 3) highlighted with a blue circle and containing the value 1. Similarly, the 'Map Section Y^ℓ' grid above it also contains integers from 0 to 3, with the pixel at position (row 1, column 3) highlighted with a blue circle and containing the value 2. From each highlighted pixel, arrows point to probability distributions: from the captured image pixel (value 1), three probabilities are shown: p_{a1,3}(2)=0.2, p_{a1,3}(1)=0.6, p_{a1,3}(0)=0.2; from the map pixel (value 2), three probabilities are shown: p_{a^ℓ_{1,3}}(3)=0.1, p_{a^ℓ_{1,3}}(2)=0.8, p_{a^ℓ_{1,3}}(1)=0.1. These represent the uncertainty in the true underlying signal values at those positions.

Below these components, a mathematical formula is displayed: p̂(x₁,x₂) += p_{a1,3}(x₁) · p_{a^ℓ_{1,3}}(x₂), with constraints x₁ ∈ {0,1,2} and x₂ ∈ {1,2,3}. This equation describes how the joint probability mass is accumulated into the empirical distribution by multiplying marginal probabilities from the captured image and map section.

On the right, the joint distribution grid has shaded cells indicating accumulated probability mass. The cell at (A=1, A^ℓ=2) is darkest, reflecting the highest probability mass, consistent with the product of the most likely values (1 from image, 2 from map). Surrounding cells have lighter shades, indicating lower but non-zero probabilities due to uncertainty. The shading visually represents the discrete probability mass assigned to each value pair (x₁,x₂) in the joint space.

Arrows connect the highlighted pixels to their respective probability distributions, which then implicitly feed into the joint distribution update via the formula. The overall workflow demonstrates how uncertainty in both data sources is modeled probabilistically and combined to build a robust empirical joint distribution, capturing the correlation between the captured image and the map.
